name: hy
desc: Dialect of Lisp that's embedded in Python
why: A Lisp dialect embedded in Python with macros and Python interop is an unusual language to try for a short while.

brief.what_it_is: Hy is a Lisp dialect embedded in Python. It takes Lisp-syntax source, either typed at a REPL or in .hy files, and transforms it into Python abstract syntax tree (AST) objects, so Python libraries can be called from Lisp code. You start an interactive REPL with the command hy, or run a program with hy myprogram.hy. The package also installs hy2py and hyc, though the README does not describe what those two do.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as wanting Lisp and Python to get along: "Lisp and Python should love each other. Let's make it happen." The practical pitch is that Hy gives you "the whole beautiful world of Python at your fingertips, in Lisp form."
brief.how_it_works: Hy reads Lisp forms and compiles them into Python AST objects, which then run on the Python runtime. Because the output is Python AST, Python modules and functions are directly usable from Hy code. The README gives no further detail on the compiler internals or macro system.

commands_seen.context: Installs the latest release of Hy into the user's Python environment, per the README's install instructions.
Runs a Hy program from a .hy file.

brief.install_notes: The README's only install instruction is pip3 install --user hy, which implies a working Python 3 with pip. No Python version, accounts, or extra configuration are mentioned. Homebrew installs three executables: hy, hy2py, and hyc.
brief.standout: Hy compiles Lisp straight to Python AST rather than to a separate runtime, so Lisp code gets full access to Python's libraries without a bridge layer. The project also has a web console at hylang.org/try-hy for trying it without installing anything.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. It names a current maintainer, Kodi Arfer, and links to an active-looking Discussions page and a PyPI version badge, but the README shows no release date, changelog, or recent commit. The Homebrew formula's scout note calls it unusual, not dead. I did not follow the docs link to check release dates.
brief.caveats: Hy runs on Python, so it inherits the Python runtime and ecosystem; it is not a standalone Lisp. The README does not discuss performance, Python version support, or which Python features are missing or differ. The README also says bug reports go to GitHub issues, and the maintainer answers questions primarily on Stack Overflow or GitHub Discussions. The license is MIT (Expat).
quotes: Lisp and Python should love each other. Let's make it happen.
Since Hy transforms its Lisp code into Python abstract syntax tree (AST) objects, you have the whole beautiful world of Python at your fingertips, in Lisp form.
We have no bugs! Your bugs are your own!

entry.title: Hy
entry.tldr: A Lisp that compiles to Python's own syntax tree, so you can write parentheses and still call any Python library.
entry.deeper_look:
Hy reads Lisp source, typed at a REPL or saved in .hy files, and turns it into Python abstract syntax tree objects. Python then runs those objects like any other Python code. Because there is no separate runtime in between, Python modules and functions are usable directly from Lisp forms.

The README states the motivation plainly: "Lisp and Python should love each other. Let's make it happen." The pitch is that you keep "the whole beautiful world of Python at your fingertips, in Lisp form."

The idea underneath is that a language can be a different front end onto an existing runtime. Python's AST is a data structure, and Hy shows what happens when you generate it from s-expressions instead of from Python's usual syntax. It is a cheap way to see how a Lisp feels when it has pip's whole ecosystem behind it.

Homebrew also installs two other executables, hy2py and hyc. The README does not say what they do, so try their --help output before assuming anything.
entry.install:
brew install hy
# Homebrew pulls in its own Python as a dependency. The README's own route is: pip3 install --user hy

try_this.what_happens: Starts an interactive REPL where you can type Lisp forms and call Python from them.
Runs a Hy program from a .hy file you have written.
Shows the options for hy2py, one of the extra executables the README leaves undescribed.

entry.whats_unique: Hy compiles straight to Python AST rather than to a separate runtime, so Lisp code gets Python's libraries without a bridge layer. There is also a web console at hylang.org/try-hy if you want to try it before installing.
entry.caveats: It is not a standalone Lisp: it runs on Python and inherits its runtime, and the README says nothing about performance or which Python features differ.
